Cure model (S(t)=π+(1−π)S∗​(t))

Words: 79
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
A cure model mixes an individual class with identically zero hazard function and a susceptible class with survivor function S∗​. For 0≤π<1, its representation as a proportional frailty model with EU=1 is U=0 with probability π and U=1/(1−π) otherwise, with baseline hazard h0​=(1−π)h∗​. The frailty law is a mixture of two Dirac measures, rather than an ordinary density. Its Laplace transform evaluated at H0​ gives the displayed survivor function. The limiting survival equals π when S∗​(t)→0; otherwise the plateau also includes susceptible individuals who never experience the event.

Survival data

Words: 65
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
Survival data describe the time T from a specified origin to an event, together with covariates and the observation mechanism. Under right censoring, the observed exit time is Y=min(T,C) and the event indicator is δ=1{T≤C}​. With left truncation, an entry time E is also recorded and subjects are observed only if T>E. Recording the time origin, entry, exit and event indicator is essential for constructing valid risk sets.

Relative survival

Words: 310 Articles: 4
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
Relative survival compares observed survival in a diseased cohort with expected survival derived from a suitable reference population. A useful individual model adds a known background mortality hazard to a common excess hazard. Reference mortality can depend on age, sex and calendar time. The comparison avoids classifying each death by cause, but its interpretation depends on the reference population being appropriate. An excess-survival ratio is not automatically the effect of a causal intervention removing one cause of death.

Relative survivor function (FE​(t)=exp[−∫0t​hE​(u)du])

Words: 143 Articles: 1
Relative survival OurBigBook.com
Under the additive hazard function model h(i)=hB(i)​+hE​, the survivor function factorization gives FE​=F(i)/FB(i)​, independently of i. If the excess hazard is nonnegative, this has a survival-probability interpretation for a hypothetical process with just that hazard. If excess hazards are negative, relative survival can exceed one and is a comparison ratio rather than an ordinary survivor function.

Risk-set-adjusted relative survivor estimator (FE​(t)=exp[∫0t​hB​(u)du]∏tj​≤t​(1−dj​/rj​))

Words: 95
Relative survivor function OurBigBook.com
With a common excess hazard, let hB​=∑i​Yi​hB(i)​/∑i​Yi​ be the known background hazard averaged over the current risk set. Estimate the excess cumulative hazard by subtracting ∫hB​ from the Nelson–Aalen estimator. Applying the product-limit construction gives the displayed estimator: the continuous background correction multiplies the ordinary Kaplan–Meier estimator. Its event jump is 1−dj​/rj​, while between events it grows at rate hB​FE​. Hence the unconstrained curve can increase, even if the true excess hazard is nonnegative. Replacing its jump factor by exp(−dj​/rj​) gives the alternative exponential cumulative-hazard estimator; these versions are close for small event fractions but are not identical.

Excess hazard (hE​(t)=h(i)(t)−hB(i)​(t))

Words: 42
Relative survival OurBigBook.com
An excess hazard measures mortality above the background hazard. When it is common across individuals, each observed survivor function factors into its individual background survivor function and a common relative survivor function. A nonnegative excess hazard gives a nonincreasing relative survivor function; a negative excess hazard can instead reflect better survival than expected in the reference population.

Background hazard (hB(i)​(t))

Words: 50
Relative survival OurBigBook.com
In relative survival, the background hazard is an individual's expected mortality hazard in a suitable reference population. Its dependence on age, sex and calendar time can be obtained from population life tables. In a heterogeneous cohort, estimating a common excess hazard requires averaging these known background hazards over the current risk set, rather than over the original cohort.

Accelerated failure time model (logTz​=μ(z)+σX,σ>0)

Words: 206 Articles: 3
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
An accelerated failure time model changes the time scale of a common event-time distribution. In a log-location-scale representation, Tz​=eμ(z)eσX with common X and positive scale σ. An additive change in μ(z) multiplies all time quantiles by the same factor. A larger time multiplier indicates longer survival, whereas a larger hazard multiplier in a proportional hazards model indicates faster failure.

Accelerated life family (Sz​(t)=S0​(t/cz​),cz​>0)

Words: 151 Articles: 2
Accelerated failure time model OurBigBook.com
An accelerated life family consists of survival distributions related by positive time scaling: Tz​ has the distribution of cz​T0​. Therefore the survivor function is Sz​(t)=S0​(t/cz​) and, for densities, the hazard function is hz​(t)=cz−1​h0​(t/cz​). This need not be a constant hazard ratio.

Negative log-scale counterexample to proportional hazards

Words: 58
Accelerated life family OurBigBook.com
For logTz​=bz−X, with eX unit exponential distribution and b=log2, the survivor functions are Sz​(t)=1−e−2z/t for t>0. These are time-scaled Fréchet distributions, so they form an accelerated life family. However their hazard ratio is 2/(e1/t+1), tending to zero as t↓0 and to one as t→∞. It is not constant. Thus a positive-scale assumption matters when deriving a proportional hazards family from the usual log-location-scale model.

Weibull accelerated-life and proportional-hazards families (Sz​(t)=exp(−λz​tk),k>0)

Words: 56
Accelerated life family OurBigBook.com
Weibull distributions with a common shape k>0 form both an accelerated life family and a proportional hazards family. Their hazard functions are hz​(t)=kλz​tk−1, whose ratio is λz​/λ0​. Their time multiplier is (λ0​/λz​)1/k. In the representation logTz​=a+bz+cX with c>0 and density ex−ex for X, the parameters are k=1/c and λz​=e−(a+bz)/c, giving time multiplier ebz and hazard multiplier e−bz/c.

Survival prediction calibration

Words: 57
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
Calibration compares predicted survival probabilities with observed survival experience at relevant horizons or over time. Censoring must be handled, for example by suitable survival estimates or inverse-probability weighting. Calibration should be assessed on validated predictions, because the fitting sample can hide optimism from variable selection and tuning. It is distinct from the risk-ranking information measured by a concordance index.

Concordance index (C)

Words: 54
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
A survival concordance index measures agreement between predicted risk ordering and observed event ordering over comparable subject pairs, with half credit for prediction ties. A pair is ordinarily comparable when the earlier observed follow-up ends in an event. Censoring-adjusted versions can reduce dependence on follow-up patterns. Good discrimination does not imply good survival prediction calibration or correct proportional hazards.

Within-patient recurrent-event dependence

Words: 53
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
Repeated episodes from one person share susceptibility, treatment and history, so row-wise independence is generally inappropriate. Patient-clustered sandwich covariance matrices estimate uncertainty using whole-patient score contributions under a suitable working model. Shared frailty models instead model persistent latent heterogeneity. These methods require independent sampling units at the patient level and do not necessarily estimate the same marginal versus conditional effect.

Gap-time recurrent-event model (g=t−tk−1​)

Words: 67
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
A gap-time model uses time since the previous recurrence as the episode clock, instead of calendar time since treatment or study entry. Subtract the previous event time from both interval endpoints. Eligibility restrictions become delayed gap entry, and patient/episode labels preserve the actual order of recurrent events. Risk sets on this clock compare eligible episodes of a common gap age, not patients at one common calendar time.

Start-stop recurrent-event data layout ((start,stop], event, id)

Words: 116 Articles: 1
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
Represent each person's successive eligible episodes by separate left-open, right-closed intervals, retaining a common patient identifier and event-order information. A recurrence ends an interval and can be followed by another one; administrative censoring ends the final interval without an event. The row's entry time determines risk set membership. Multiple rows remain one patient history, with possible within-patient recurrent-event dependence.

Refractory period in recurrent-event analysis (Yi​(t)=0(tk​<t<tk​+r))

Words: 61
Start-stop recurrent-event data layout OurBigBook.com
A refractory period makes a patient ineligible for another event for a fixed time r after a recurrence. Exclude this time from exposure and risk sets by delaying the next interval's entry to tk​+r. In a gap-time recurrent-event model measured from the previous event, the next interval enters at gap age r, not zero; the clock is not reset at the end of recovery.

Survival time (T)

Words: 82 Articles: 1
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
A survival time is the elapsed time to an event of interest, which may be death, failure, recovery or completion of a task. Its survival function and hazard function describe the event-time law. Right censoring records only that the event time exceeds the observed follow-up time.

Survival distribution

Words: 42
Survival time OurBigBook.com
A survival distribution is the probability distribution of an event or failure time, commonly summarized by its survivor function, hazard function or cumulative hazard function. It may contain atoms or a positive probability of an event never occurring; an ordinary density-based hazard therefore need not describe every survival distribution.

Cox–Snell residual (ri​=Hi​(xi​))

Words: 218 Articles: 3
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
A Cox–Snell residual is the fitted cumulative hazard function evaluated at an observed event or censoring time. Under a correct model, complete transformed event times are unit exponential; censored transformed times retain their event indicators. A logarithmic Kaplan–Meier estimator survivor plot should be close to a line of slope minus one.

Cox–Snell residual survival diagnostic (Sr​(r)≈e−r)

Words: 148 Articles: 1
Cox–Snell residual OurBigBook.com
For a correct fitted survival law, complete Cox–Snell residuals are approximately unit exponential. Residuals computed at observed censored times retain their censoring indicators. Fit a Kaplan–Meier estimator to the transformed times and indicators and compare it with e−r, or compare their Nelson–Aalen estimator cumulative hazard with r. Treating censored transformed times as complete exponential observations gives a distorted Q–Q check.

Shared-fit Cox–Snell residuals reproduce the fitted survival curve

Words: 92
Cox–Snell residual survival diagnostic OurBigBook.com
If a common Kaplan–Meier estimator S is fitted and the same data are transformed to ui​=−logS(xi​) with censoring indicators retained, event ordering and risk sets are preserved under compatible tie conventions. At a transformed event time uj​, the residual product-limit estimate equals S(xj​)=e−uj​. Consequently agreement of the pooled residual curve with the exponential target is largely built into the construction. Separate group curves or a model fitted with covariates can reveal differences concealed by the pooled fit. Residuals become infinite if the fitted survivor reaches zero.

Modified Cox–Snell residual (Y∗=H(min(T,C))+1−Δ)

Words: 26
Cox–Snell residual OurBigBook.com
For an observed transformed time Y=H(min(T,C)) and event indicator Δ, the correction Y∗=Y+1−Δ has mean one under independent censoring. Its complement 1−Y∗=Δ−Y is the corresponding martingale residual.

Gompertz distribution (h(t)=qeβt)

Words: 38
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
A positive, exponentially increasing hazard function h(t)=qeβt gives the survivor function
S(t)=exp[−βq​(eβt−1)],q,β>0.
(1)
Its mean is β−1eq/βE1​(q/β), where E1​ is the exponential integral. Unlike the exponential distribution, its future mean waiting time is not the reciprocal of its current hazard function.

Survival function (S(t))

Words: 686 Articles: 14
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
For an event time T, the survival function is S(t)=P(T>t)=1−F(t), up to the endpoint convention used for atoms.

Mean residual life (mX​(t)=E[X−t∣X>t])

Words: 50
Survival function OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative random variable with finite expected value and P(X>t)>0, its mean residual life is the remaining conditional expected value after surviving past t. The tail integral formula for moments gives mX​(t)=∫t∞​P(X>x)dx/P(X>t). The exponential distribution has constant mean residual life, equal to its original mean. In excess of loss reinsurance, the total variance stationary condition for excess of loss sets a candidate retention equal to this quantity.

Restricted mean survival time (RMST(τ)=∫0τ​S(t)dt)

Words: 47
Survival function OurBigBook.com
The restricted mean survival time to a fixed cutoff τ is E[min(T,τ)]=∫0τ​S(t)dt for a nonnegative event time. This follows by the tail integral formula for moments. Unlike the unrestricted mean, it uses no tail beyond τ; under independent censoring it can be estimated by integrating a Kaplan–Meier estimator over adequately observed follow-up.

Hazard function (h(t))

Words: 568 Articles: 11
Survival function OurBigBook.com
The hazard function is the instantaneous event rate conditional on survival to time t. For an absolutely continuous distribution, h(t)=f(t)/S(t).

Poisson record counts in cumulative hazard coordinates (Rt​∼Poisson(−log(1−F(t))))

Words: 77
Hazard function OurBigBook.com
Upper records of iid observations with a continuous distribution have transition density f(w)/(1−F(v)) above the latest record v. Consequently the cumulative hazard Λ(v)=−log(1−F(v)) transforms consecutive record increments into independent unit exponentials. Record counts below a level t with F(t)<1 are therefore Poisson with mean Λ(t). Set the count to zero if the first record exceeds the level. At a finite upper endpoint with F(t)=1, the count is infinite instead of a finite-mean Poisson variable.

Discrete hazard (hj​=P(T=tj​∣T>tj−1​))

Words: 51
Hazard function OurBigBook.com
At ordered possible failure times tj​, the discrete hazard is hj​=P(T=tj​∣T>tj−1​). Its survival function satisfies S(tj​)=S(tj−1​)(1−hj​), and hence S(t)=∏tj​≤t​(1−hj​). Estimating hj​ by the observed number of failures divided by the risk set size under independent censoring yields the Kaplan–Meier estimator. Unlike a continuous-time hazard rate, a discrete hazard is a probability between zero and one.

Population hazard of a survival mixture (h(t)=∑i​Fi​(t)∑i​Fi​(t)hi​(t)​)

Words: 241 Articles: 3
Hazard function OurBigBook.com
For an equally weighted mixture of individual survivor functions Fi​, the population hazard function is h(t)=∑i​Fi​(t)hi​(t)/∑i​Fi​(t). Thus the weights are the surviving proportions, and the cumulative hazard function is −log(n−1∑i​e−Hi​(t)), not generally the mean individual integrated hazard.
Decreasing population hazard under constant individual hazards (h′(t)=−Var(Λ∣T>t)≤0)
Words: 61
Population hazard of a survival mixture OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative random constant individual hazard Λ, write Mk​(t)=E[Λke−Λt]. The population survivor function is M0​ and its hazard is M1​/M0​. Under the integrability needed to differentiate, Mk′​=−Mk+1​, so
h′=M02​−M2​M0​+M12​​=−Var(Λ∣T>t).
(2)
The conditional distribution is weighted by e−Λt. This proves decreasing population hazard without any decrease in individual hazards and explains survival selection in a heterogeneous population.
Survival selection in a heterogeneous population (wi​(t)=∑j​pj​Sj​(t)pi​Si​(t)​)
Words: 66
Population hazard of a survival mixture OurBigBook.com
In a population mixture with initial component probabilities pi​, conditioning on survival to time t changes them to the displayed probabilities by Bayes' theorem. Components with larger survivor functions receive greater relative weight among survivors. The population hazard function is the weighted mean of the component hazards with these time-dependent weights. This selection can change the population hazard even when all component hazards are constant, as shown by the hazard derivative for a mixture of exponential distributions.
Hazard derivative for a mixture of exponential distributions (h′(t)=−Var(Λ∣T>t))
Words: 77
Population hazard of a survival mixture OurBigBook.com
For a finite mixture with positive weights pi​ and rates λi​>0, the survivor function is S(t)=∑i​pi​e−λi​t and the hazard function is the surviving-population mean of the component rates. Write wi​(t)=pi​e−λi​t/S(t). Differentiation gives wi′​=wi​(h−λi​) and therefore h′=h2−∑i​wi​λi2​=−Var(Λ∣T>t). The hazard is decreasing, strictly so when distinct rates have positive weights. For finitely many rates it tends to the smallest rate with positive weight. This is survival selection even though each individual component has a constant hazard.

Mean accumulated hazard under independent censoring (EH(min(T,C))=P(T≤C))
Words: 72
Cumulative hazard function OurBigBook.com
Let X=min(T,C), V=1{T≤C}​, and suppose T and C are independent, with continuous failure density f=hS. Then the Tonelli theorem gives
EH(X)=∫0∞​h(t)S(t)P(C≥t)dt=P(T≤C)=EV.
(3)
Thus V−H(X) has mean zero. The identity also holds conditionally on covariates when censoring is independent conditionally on them. For an estimated hazard, the mean error is controlled by E∣H(X)−H(X)∣, not by pointwise fit alone.

Mean accumulated hazard before fixed censoring (EH(min(T,c))=P(T≤c))
Words: 57
Cumulative hazard function OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative continuous event time with survival function S, hazard function h and H the cumulative hazard, split the expectation at c. The censored contribution is S(c)H(c). The event contribution is ∫0c​H(t)f(t)dt=1−S(c)−S(c)H(c) by integration by parts, since dH=hdt and f=hS. Adding gives the displayed identity. Linearity extends it to the expected observed event count in a cohort, without requiring independence between subjects.

For a proper continuous event time and invertible cumulative hazard function H, the survivor function identity F(t)=e−H(t) gives H(T)∼Exp(1).

Additive excess-hazard mixture likelihood

Words: 72
Survival likelihood OurBigBook.com
Suppose an unobserved class has probabilities π and 1−π, with hazard functions q and q+r, and set Q(t)=∫0t​q, R(t)=∫0t​r. For an independently right-censored observation (x,v), its survival-parameter likelihood contribution is
L=e−Q(x){πq(x)v+(1−π)[q(x)+r(x)]ve−R(x)}.
(4)
This sums the two class-specific likelihoods before taking a logarithm. All hazards must be nonnegative. A common parameter-free censoring mechanism factors out; class-specific censoring instead alters the mixture weights and cannot silently be discarded.

Survival likelihood OurBigBook.com
Under independent censoring and a constant event rate, d observed events over total observed person-time X give likelihood proportional to λde−λX and estimate d/X for d,X>0. Censored observations belong in X. With no events the positive-rate likelihood has a boundary supremum.

Informative censoring occurs when censoring carries information about the future event time beyond the variables conditioned on in the analysis. It can invalidate ordinary Kaplan–Meier estimator and survival-model residual interpretations.

If a cohort is periodically confirmed event-free but exact event reports update only those who fail, censoring the remaining subjects at their last scheduled confirmation creates informative censoring. Between confirmations the nominal risk set retains future observed failures and removes nonfailures. An apparent final failure may therefore empty the recorded risk set even though other cohort members remain event-free. Use a common verified cutoff or a complete event register with a common administrative censoring date.

Independent censoring means that, conditional on the variables used in the analysis, the censoring time carries no further information about the event time. It lets the observed risk set represent those who would remain at risk without censoring.

A censoring flag chosen independently of the recorded duration does not establish independent censoring of a latent failure time. Stratified log-rank statistic OurBigBook.com
With one A and one B observation per stratum and no ties, the stratified log-rank statistic receives a nonzero contribution only when the earlier observation is a failure while both remain at risk. It is +1/2 if A fails first and −1/2 if B fails first. After the first observation, only one member remains and every further observed-minus-expected contribution is zero. Its E-step uses the displayed conditional weights and the first two moments of a truncated normal distribution above logc. The M-step updates each class probability to its average weight, its mean to the weighted first moment, and its variance to the weighted second moment minus the squared new mean. The time function is evaluated at the current event/risk-set time, not each person's eventual outcome time. Scaled Schoenfeld residuals provide related graphical and score-test diagnostics for coefficient trends.

Schoenfeld residual (sj​=xij​​−∑i∈Rj​​exiT​β​∑i∈Rj​​xi​exiT​β​​)

Words: 96 Articles: 1
Cox proportional-hazards model OurBigBook.com
At an untied event time, a Schoenfeld residual is the event subject's covariate vector minus its fitted risk-weighted average over the risk set. Under a correctly specified Cox proportional-hazards model, these residuals have no systematic mean trend with event time. They are defined at event times, unlike Cox–Snell residuals which can be evaluated at both events and censoring times.

Scaled Schoenfeld residual

Words: 42
Schoenfeld residual OurBigBook.com
A scaled Schoenfeld residual rescales a Schoenfeld residual using fitted information so that its trend can diagnose departures from a constant coefficient in a Cox proportional-hazards model. A smooth trend against transformed event time estimates a time-dependent coefficient pattern; a flat trend supports the working proportional hazards assumption test.

Cox partial likelihood

Words: 358 Articles: 5
Cox proportional-hazards model OurBigBook.com
The Cox partial likelihood conditions each event on its risk set, eliminating the baseline hazard.

Score and information of Cox partial likelihood (U(β)=∑j​[zij​​−zˉj​(β)],I(β)=∑j​Covwj​​(z))

Words: 59
Cox partial likelihood OurBigBook.com
At an untied event time, the Cox partial likelihood weights the current risk set by wjk​=eβTzk​/∑ℓ∈Rj​​eβTzℓ​. Differentiation gives the displayed score function and the negative Hessian as a sum of weighted covariances. The score is the sum of Schoenfeld functions, so Schoenfeld residuals sum to zero at a finite interior unpenalized fit. At arbitrary trial coefficients or boundary fits, a zero sum is not a general identity.

Exact tied-set conditional likelihood (LD​=∑A⊆R,∣A∣=d​∏i∈A​ui​∏i∈D​ui​​)

Words: 71
Cox partial likelihood OurBigBook.com
In a discrete-time model with independent event indicators whose odds are aui​, condition on exactly d events in the risk set R. The common factor ad cancels and the conditional probability of the event set D is the displayed ratio. The denominator is an elementary symmetric polynomial and can be evaluated by recursion rather than enumerating every subset. This conditional model is distinct from summing a continuous-time rank likelihood over all unobserved within-tie orders.

Efron approximation for tied event times (∏q=0d−1​(S−qUD​/d)∏i∈D​ui​​)

Words: 67
Cox partial likelihood OurBigBook.com
For d events tied within a risk set, put ui​=exp(βTzi​), S=∑i∈R​ui​ and UD​=∑i∈D​ui​. The Efron approximation to Cox partial likelihood removes the average tied-event hazard multiplier from the denominator at each successive event. Unlike the Breslow approximation for tied event times, it accounts approximately for depletion of the risk set within the group. Factors independent of β can be dropped for estimation. This is an approximation for coarsened continuous event times, not a full interval-observation likelihood.

Breslow approximation for tied event times ((∑i∈Rj​​exiT​β)dj​exp(∑i∈Dj​​xiT​β)​)

Words: 44
Cox partial likelihood OurBigBook.com
When dj​ events occur at the same recorded time, the Breslow approximation to Cox partial likelihood uses the factor exp(∑i∈Dj​​xiT​β)/(∑i∈Rj​​exiT​β)dj​, where Rj​ is the risk set and Dj​ the event set. It approximates the ordering of tied events rather than treating their within-tie order as known.

Cox rank-likelihood deletion consistency

Words: 102
Cox partial likelihood OurBigBook.com
Assume independent individual event times with positive time-constant hazard multipliers and a common baseline hazard whose cumulative hazard tends to infinity. Transforming each event time by that cumulative hazard then gives independent exponential event times with corresponding rates, so all event orders exist. Their complete-order probabilities select each next label proportionally to its remaining multiplier. Marginalizing over the position of a deleted label leaves the order law of the other exponential times, hence the same sequential formula without that label. This proves the deletion identity used when unobserved ranks are summed out. It does not supply a likelihood function for censoring times; ignoring censoring in observed survival analysis still needs independent censoring.

Breslow estimator (H0​(t))

Words: 31
Cox proportional-hazards model OurBigBook.com
The Breslow estimator of the baseline cumulative hazard in a Cox proportional-hazards model adds the observed number of events at each event time divided by the sum of fitted relative risks in its risk set.

Stratified Cox model

Words: 73 Articles: 2
Cox proportional-hazards model OurBigBook.com
A stratified Cox model gives each stratum its own baseline hazard while sharing regression coefficients.

First-event versus recurrent-event baseline stratification

Words: 48
Stratified Cox model OurBigBook.com
Separate first-event episodes from all later episodes with a stratum indicator. A Stratified Cox model permits one baseline hazard for first events and another for recurrent events while retaining a common treatment coefficient. Later episodes can share their baseline; stratifying each recurrence number separately is a stronger model than the first-versus-later distinction alone.

Stratum

Words: 10
Stratified Cox model OurBigBook.com
A stratum is a subgroup assigned its own nuisance baseline.

Truncation (statistics)

Words: 32 Articles: 1
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
Truncation omits observations outside a specified range, so the analyst does not observe that those population members were sampled.

Left truncation

Words: 13
Truncation (statistics) OurBigBook.com
Left truncation includes an individual only after survival to a delayed entry time.

Kaplan–Meier estimator

Words: 709 Articles: 10
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
The Kaplan–Meier product-limit estimator multiplies factors 1−dj​/nj​ over event times.

Kaplan–Meier median survival time (m=inf{t:S(t)≤1/2})

Words: 59
Kaplan–Meier estimator OurBigBook.com
The median survival estimate is the first event time at which the Kaplan–Meier estimator reaches or falls below one half. It is not identified beyond the observed follow-up if the curve never reaches that level. A few reported survival probabilities bound the crossing time but do not determine an exact median. Confidence intervals can be constructed by inverting confidence bands for the survivor function.

Constrained Kaplan–Meier estimator (∏sj​≤t​(1−qj​)=p)

Words: 122
Kaplan–Meier estimator OurBigBook.com
The Kaplan–Meier estimator constrained to have survivor function value p∈(0,1) at t maximizes the right-censoring log-likelihood ∑j​[dj​logqj​+(nj​−dj​)log(1−qj​)] subject to the displayed constraint. Here qj​ is the discrete hazard, dj​ the event count and nj​ the risk set size. In an interior event-time solution, a Lagrange multiplier gives qj​=dj​/(nj​+λ) before the constrained time, with qj​=dj​/nj​ afterwards. The multiplier is chosen to satisfy the product constraint. It is essential to allow a zero-event jump at the constrained time or another relevant cell boundary: a constraint can require mass outside observed event times. A general implementation instead maximizes the concave probability-mass log-likelihood with total mass one and mass above t equal to p, allowing all relevant cells and a terminal tail. This also handles unobserved tails and boundary solutions without imposing unjustified event-only support.

Kaplan–Meier telescoping across a censor-free interval (S(b)=S(a)(r−d)/r)

Words: 67
Kaplan–Meier estimator OurBigBook.com
For a fixed cohort with r individuals at risk just after a, no censoring or entry inside (a,b), and d events in (a,b], the Kaplan–Meier estimator factors telescope to the displayed ratio. A tied group of dj​ events contributes (rj​−dj​)/rj​, the same product as any sequential ordering without intervening censoring. Events at b are counted before censoring at the same time under the usual convention.

Greenwood formula (Var(S(t)))

Words: 82
Kaplan–Meier estimator OurBigBook.com
For the Kaplan–Meier estimator, the estimated variance is
Var(S(t))=S(t)2∑tj​≤t​rj​(rj​−dj​)dj​​.
(12)
The formula follows by summing approximate variances of the logarithms of the conditional survival factors and applying the delta method to their product. Its square root is the estimated standard error. The same expression uses the actual delayed-entry risk sets for the Kaplan–Meier estimator with delayed entry. When 0<S(t)<1 and every contributing rj​>dj​, an approximate log-scale confidence interval is exp{logS(t)±z1−α/2​se(S(t))/S(t)}, with the upper endpoint capped at one. This interval can be inaccurate with very small risk sets.

Kaplan–Meier estimator with delayed entry (S(t))

Words: 100
Kaplan–Meier estimator OurBigBook.com
For independently left-truncated and right-censored survival data, let Ei​ and Yi​ be entry and exit times on the same clock. At each distinct event time tj​, the risk set is Rj​={i:Ei​<tj​≤Yi​}, with size rj​, and dj​ events occur. The Kaplan–Meier estimator is
S(t)=∏tj​≤t​(1−rj​dj​​).
(13)
Before entry a subject contributes neither an event nor time at risk. Thus adding observed entrants can increase successive risk sets; pretending that all subjects were observed from time zero distorts the estimated hazard function. The estimator identifies the survival function over ages covered by observation; normalization from birth requires observation arbitrarily close to time zero or additional knowledge of earlier survival.

Self-consistency of Kaplan–Meier estimation

Words: 30
Kaplan–Meier estimator OurBigBook.com
The Kaplan–Meier estimator is self-consistent under fractional allocation of censored event times according to its own conditional fitted event distribution. Adding the corresponding fractional event counts and risk set weights leaves the estimator unchanged.

Fractional event imputation

Words: 37
Kaplan–Meier estimator OurBigBook.com
If a censored individual is allocated event weights qj​ over later event times, its event-count contribution at time tj​ is qj​ and its risk set contribution is ∑k≥j​qk​. These fractional counts can be used in the Kaplan–Meier estimator.

Terminal censoring and survival-mean identifiability

Words: 113
Kaplan–Meier estimator OurBigBook.com
If the last observed follow-up is a censoring time and the Kaplan–Meier estimator remains positive there, the observed curve does not determine the remaining tail area. Many possible completions give different full means, including finite and infinite ones. A horizontal plotting extension is not proof that the true mean is infinite. If the final risk set is exhausted by events, its Kaplan–Meier estimator factor is zero and the conventional fitted curve has finite area. This includes a unique last individual having an event, but an event tied with terminal censoring can leave a positive fitted survivor value when events are processed before censoring. The random endpoint still does not establish a population support bound. A restricted mean survival time avoids unsupported tail completion.

Potential right-censoring time

Words: 46
Kaplan–Meier estimator OurBigBook.com
A grid of potential right censoring times includes every observed censoring time. Intervals between consecutive grid points have no internal censoring, so their Kaplan–Meier estimator factors telescope to a single ratio of event-free survivors to individuals observed across the interval. This gives the same estimator when endpoint risk sets are counted consistently.

Potential event time

Words: 43
Kaplan–Meier estimator OurBigBook.com
A potential event time is a support point permitted in the discrete event-time distribution used to derive the Kaplan–Meier estimator by maximum likelihood estimation. The support must include every observed exact event time. Additional points with a nonempty risk set but no observed event receive zero fitted event mass.

Words: 435 Articles: 6
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
The Nelson–Aalen estimator of the cumulative hazard is H(t)=∑tj​≤t​dj​/rj​, where dj​ events occur among rj​ individuals at risk at event time tj​.

Small-jump comparison of cumulative hazard estimators (−log(1−u)−u=21​u2+O(u3))

Words: 63
Nelson–Aalen estimator OurBigBook.com
At a failure time with d events among r at risk, the Nelson–Aalen estimator adds u=d/r, whereas minus the logarithm of the Kaplan–Meier estimator adds −log(1−u). For 0≤u<1,
0≤−log(1−u)−u=∑m=2∞​mum​≤2(1−u)u2​.
(14)
Thus small event fractions give close cumulative hazard estimates. Large risk sets alone do not suffice when a large fraction fail together. If all remaining individuals fail, the logarithmic estimate becomes infinite while the Nelson–Aalen jump is one.

Offset-adjusted cumulative hazard estimator (H1​=∫YdN−∑i​Yi​h0i​dt​)

Words: 101
Nelson–Aalen estimator OurBigBook.com
Suppose individual event hazards have the additive form hi​=h0i​+h1​, where h0i​ is known and h1​ is common. The aggregate counting-process intensity in survival analysis is λ=∑i​Yi​h0i​+Yh1​, with Y=∑i​Yi​ the current risk set size. Writing dN=λdt+dM and dividing by Y gives
H1​(t)=∫0t​Y1{Y>0}​​dN−∫0t​1{Y>0}​Y∑i​Yi​h0i​​du=∫0t​1{Y>0}​h1​du+∫0t​Y1{Y>0}​​dM.
(15)
The last term is a counting-process martingale integral. This establishes the cumulative common-hazard target on the observed at-risk time range. The known offset must be averaged over the current risk set, not the initial sample. Between event jumps, its subtraction can make the unconstrained estimate decrease. If all known hazards equal h0​ and Y>0 up to t, the estimate reduces to the Nelson–Aalen estimator minus H0​(t).

Event-count identity for Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazards (∑i​H(xi​)=d)

Words: 136 Articles: 1
Nelson–Aalen estimator OurBigBook.com
With all subjects entering at time zero and no tied observation times, the Nelson–Aalen estimator satisfies ∑i​H(xi​)=d. Exchanging sums makes each event increment 1/Y(tj​) appear in exactly Y(tj​) subject hazards. The identity relies on the risk-set count equalling the number of observation times at least tj​, and generally needs modification for delayed entry.

Grouped Nelson–Aalen event-count identity (∑j​nj​H(tj​)=∑j​dj​)

Words: 82
Event-count identity for Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazards OurBigBook.com
Suppose everyone enters observation at zero and has one event or censoring time. At distinct recorded time tj​, let nj​ observations terminate, of which dj​ are events, and use the pre-time risk set size rj​=∑k≥j​nk​. For the grouped Nelson–Aalen estimator, H(tj​)=∑k≤j​dk​/rk​. Exchanging sums gives ∑j​nj​H(tj​)=∑k​(dk​/rk​)∑j≥k​nj​=∑k​dk​. The unweighted sum over distinct times generally does not have this property. Processing each observation separately after breaking ties also restores the corresponding unweighted identity on the resulting artificial time grid.

Nelson–Aalen variance estimator (V(t)=∑aj​≤t​Yj−2​)

Words: 52
Nelson–Aalen estimator OurBigBook.com
For untied events at aj​ with predictable risk set size Yj​, the estimated predictable variation of the Nelson–Aalen estimator is ∑aj​≤t​Yj−2​. It comes from the martingale event increment variance YdH and the estimator increment dN/Y. It applies on the range with individuals at risk; it is not an exact finite-sample unbiasedness statement.

Finite-sample bias of Nelson–Aalen estimation

Words: 57
Nelson–Aalen estimator OurBigBook.com
Even with a common event hazard, the exact expectation of the Nelson–Aalen estimator is ∫0t​P(Y(u)>0)h(u)du, because no increments can be observed after the risk set is empty. Replacing ratios by ratios of expectations gives an approximate target and does not prove finite-sample unbiasedness. For one uncensored exponential event time, the estimator has mean 1−e−λt rather than λt.

Martingale residual (Mi​)

Words: 163 Articles: 2
Survival analysis OurBigBook.com
A martingale residual is the observed event count minus its fitted cumulative intensity. In a survival model, Mi​=Ni​(τ)−Λi​(τ) compares whether individual i experienced an event with the event count predicted over that individual's follow-up.

Terminal-observation invariance of Cox martingale residuals (Mi​=vi​−eβ​Tzi​H0​(xi​))

Words: 84
Martingale residual OurBigBook.com
In an untied Cox proportional-hazards model with a single subject remaining after all other observed exit times, that subject's event contributes the constant factor one to Cox partial likelihood. Replacing its terminal censoring time by a later event therefore preserves the fitted coefficients and every earlier Breslow estimator increment. At its new event, the subject's fitted cumulative hazard increases by one, cancelling the increase of one in its event indicator. Every martingale residual is unchanged. This property relies on the subject being alone in the terminal risk set and the same covariate history being retained.

Zero sum of Cox martingale residuals

Words: 44
Martingale residual OurBigBook.com
When a Cox proportional-hazards model uses the Breslow estimator, the sum of fitted martingale residuals is zero. Each estimated baseline hazard jump redistributes one observed event across its risk set, so summing cumulative fitted intensities equals summing observed event counts. The identity holds for any finite regression coefficient used consistently in both calculations.

Period survival analysis estimates survival under the event hazards operating during a recent calendar period by combining appropriately left-truncated and right-censored portions of several follow-up cohorts.

A constant hazard survival model takes h(t)=λ, giving survivor function S(t)=e−λt and an exponential event-time distribution.

For independent exponentially distributed failure times subject to independent right censoring, let d be observed failures and E=∑i​xi​ total follow-up exposure. The parameter-dependent likelihood is θde−θE, giving maximum-likelihood estimator θ=d/E. The fitted individual cumulative hazards sum to d, but this estimating identity alone does not establish that a constant hazard model fits.

A piecewise-exponential model takes the hazard to be constant on fixed time intervals.

Piecewise-exponential survival model OurBigBook.com
For specified exposure periods with constant death hazard functions hk​, the integrated hazard through the endpoint is ∑k​hk​Δtk​. The displayed event probability follows from the survivor function identity. For different latent exposure schedules mixed with probabilities wj​, average the schedule-specific probabilities, ∑j​wj​(1−e−Hj​), rather than exponentiating the average integrated hazard. When the hazards are small, 1−e−Hj​≃Hj​ gives a person-time approximation. A comparison must specify the entire custody or treatment schedule; later changes to exposure cannot be inferred from an endpoint rate alone.
